opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that a research career is long. If you're lucky, you're doing this for forty or fifty years, and the field you started in won't look anything like the field you end up in. When I started in computer vision in the 1980s, the dominant ideas were edge detection, geometry, and hand-designed features. Then came the statistical machine learning era, then deep learning around 2012, and now we're in a world of large-scale self-supervised models and the connections between vision, language, and robotics. If I had insisted on staying with the techniques I learned as a graduate student, I would have become irrelevant a long time ago.

But I want to separate two things: the problems and the methods. I've been fairly constant about the problems. I've always cared about how we perceive the world, how we recognize objects, understand scenes, and how perception connects to action. Those are deep, long-lived questions. What has to be fluid are the tools. A researcher should be loyal to the question, not to the hammer.

This is hard psychologically. When you've built a reputation on a certain approach, there's a strong temptation to defend it. I've seen very good people get stuck because a new paradigm threatened their life's work. When convolutional networks showed those dramatic results on ImageNet, some of us had to say, honestly, "this works better than what we were doing," and then go learn it, and ideally contribute something to it. That's humbling, but it's also exciting. You get to be a student again.

There's also a practical side. Each paradigm shift opens up questions the previous one couldn't address. Moving toward robotics and embodied learning, for example, has been very energizing for me, because I think perception doesn't fully make sense divorced from action. You only get to explore that if you're willing to step outside your comfort zone.

So my advice to young researchers is: build deep foundations in mathematics, in the fundamentals, and in a real understanding of the problem domain, because those transfer. Then hold your specific methods lightly. Be ready to reinvent yourself every decade or so. That's not a sign of inconsistency; it's what keeps you doing meaningful work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that insisting on the techniques learned as a graduate student would have made the speaker irrelevant.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes researchers getting stuck defending approaches tied to their reputation or life's work, and says they had to accept when a new paradigm worked better and learn it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the field itself doesn't stay still. I've been working in computer vision for over four decades now, and the computer vision I was doing as a graduate student at Stanford in the early eighties bears very little resemblance to what we do today. We were working with a few hundred images, hand-designing features, trying to reason about edges and geometry. Then came the statistical learning era, then deep learning, and now large models trained on internet-scale data. If I had insisted on doing things the way I learned them in 1985, I would have become irrelevant a long time ago.

So adaptability for me is partly just intellectual honesty. When the evidence shows that an approach works better, you have to be willing to say, okay, my previous way of thinking was wrong or at least incomplete, and I need to learn this new thing. I remember around 2012, when the AlexNet results came out, there were a lot of senior people in the field who were skeptical, and I confess I had my own doubts. But the results were the results. And I made a conscious decision to really engage with it, to have my students work on it, to understand it deeply rather than dismiss it. Some of the most productive years of my career came after that.

The second aspect is that the problems you care about should drive you, not the techniques. I've always been interested in perception, in how a system can understand the visual world, and I've been willing to move around in terms of methods to make progress on that. That's different from being fickle. There's a distinction between chasing fashion and being responsive to what actually works. The problem gives you a stable center, and adaptability is about the means.

And the third thing I'd say is that adaptability is what keeps the work fun. If you're doing the same thing for forty years, it's a job. If every five or ten years you're essentially a student again, learning something new, being a bit uncomfortable, that's what makes it a career worth having. I tell my students that the most important skill they'll leave with is not any particular technique but the ability to learn the next one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that insisting on doing research the way they learned it in 1985 would have made them irrelevant.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes recognizing when a previous way of thinking is wrong or incomplete, learning a new approach, and moving beyond methods that no longer fit the field.

astra-6.text:
Research is about working on things we don’t yet understand, so you have to be prepared to change your mind. You may start with a beautiful idea, but if the evidence doesn’t support it, you have to let it go. And sometimes a new tool or a new discovery makes a question tractable that you couldn’t have approached before.

That’s why adaptability matters over a career. You can’t simply keep doing what made you successful ten or twenty years ago. You need to keep learning, including from your students, and be willing to become a beginner again. What should remain constant is your curiosity and your standards for evidence; the methods and even the questions can change.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers cannot rely on what made them successful years ago and that methods can change, but it does not state that sticking with a mastered technique leads to obsolescence.

r002.rationale: The response says to let go of an idea when evidence does not support it and that methods or questions can change, but it does not state that adapting may require abandoning approaches invested in for years when they become irrelevant.

sol-6.1.text:
Research is about stepping into the unknown, so you have to be willing to change your mind. You may start with a particular problem or a particular approach, but as you learn more, you discover that your assumptions were wrong, or that a different question is more interesting. If you remain attached to your original plan, you can miss the opportunity.

There’s also the fact that a research career spans decades. The tools change, the important problems change, and other people make discoveries that alter what is possible. You want to have some enduring intellectual interests, but you shouldn’t confuse those interests with loyalty to a particular technique. The goal is to understand something, and that means being willing to learn new ways of thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should not stay loyal to one technique as tools change, but it does not state that clinging to a previously mastered technique leads to obsolescence.

r002.rationale: It recommends changing approaches when assumptions are wrong or another question is more interesting, but does not say researchers may need to abandon approaches built over years when those approaches become irrelevant.
